(1)
In the Supreme Court of the United States

No. 25-5930
WILLIAM MAXWELL, PETITIONER
v.
SANDRA DINIS, ACTING WARDEN

ON WRIT OF CERTIORARI
TO THE UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS
FOR THE FIFTH CIRCUIT

REPLY BRIEF FOR THE RESPONDENT

The Fifth Circuit held that a prisoner’s claim seeking
transfer to prerelease custody  in a halfway house or
home confinement based on time credits under the First
Step Act of 2018, Pub. L. No. 115 -391, 132 Stat. 5194 ,
must be brought in “a civil rights suit ” under Bivens v.
Six Unknown Named Agents of the Federal Bureau of
Narcotics , 403 U.S. 388 (1971), and that a habeas suit
under 28 U.S.C. 2241 “is not the proper vehicle” for such
a claim .  J.A. 35.  The Court -appointed amicus curiae
rightly declines  (Br. 41 -42) to defend the first half of
that holding .  And his defense of the second half  is unpersuasive.  This Court’s precedents establish that a claim
alleging unlawfully prolonged imprisonment and seeking release from prison into the community  is properly
brought in habeas.   See, e.g., Jones v. Hendrix, 599 U.S.
465, 475 (2023) ; Preiser v. Rodriguez , 411 U.S. 475, 500
(1973).  Amicus accordingly  acknowledges  that habeas

2

encompasses  “claims to end or shorten a prisoner’s
physical detention ,” Br. 14; see Br. 20 , which is exactly
what petitioner’s time-credits claim seeks to do: shorten
his confinement  in federal prison and thereby obtain
“speedier release into the community,” Wilkinson  v.
Dotson, 544 U.S. 74, 82 (2005).
Amicus’s contrary view rests on the unlikely  proposition that a person in prerelease custody  in a halfway
house or even in his own home —who is allowed to come
and go for such varied purposes as “ job-related” or
“job -seeking activities,” “community service,” “religious activities,” and “family-related activities,” 18 U.S.C.
3624(g)(2)(A)(i)(II)(aa), (cc), (ff  ), and (gg) —remains in
“physical detention” equivalent to  prison.  See Amicus
Br. 9 ( “a prisoner in Prerelease Custody is  *  * *  imprisoned ”); id. at 25 (“[t]he ‘level of custody’ in Prerelease Custody is the same as in prison”) .  That is wrong
as a matter of both law and common sense.   Habeas is
the proper vehicle for petitioner’s claim because he alleges that he has been unlawfully deprived of time credits that would shorten his confinement in prison, and he
seeks as a remedy accelerated transfer out of prison and
into prerelease custody in the community.
To be sure, a micus is correct about several other
points.  He correctly resists (Br. 16-20) extending habeas
to “conditions of confinement” claims  and counsels  (Br.
34-37) against petitioner’s suggestion  that habeas
should encompass all challenges to a prisoner’s “level of
custody.”  Amicus also correctly  recognizes that “Congress appears to have barred ” judicial review of First
Step Act claims like petitioner’s in 18 U.S.C. 3621(b) ,
Br. 40; see Br. 41,  which ultimately makes it of little
practical importan ce whether such claims should sound
in habeas .  See Gov’t Br. 36-40.  But with respect to  the
question presented, amicus  only reinforces the flaws in

3

the Fifth Circuit’s  threadbare analysis.  Therefore, absent dismissal of  the writ of certiorari as improvidently
granted, the judgment of the court of appeals should be
vacated.
A. Claims Challenging Unlawfully Prolonged Confinement
In Prison Are Cognizable In Habeas
1. The government’s standard is correct and workable
a. As we explained in our opening brief (at 21 -24),
this Court’s cases establish a clear rule:  Habeas is the
proper vehicle for a prisoner’s claim alleging that he is
being subjected  to unlawfully prolonged confinement in
prison and seeking immediate or accelerated release
into the community.  “In England, as in the United States,
the chief use of habeas corpus has been to seek the release of persons held in actual, physical custody in
prison or jail.”   Jones v. Cunningham , 371 U.S. 236, 238
(1963).  In Preiser v. Rodriguez , 411 U.S. 475  (1973),
this Court applied that principle to  state prisoners who
alleged that they had been wrongfully deprived of “goodconduct-time credits ” and who sought to have those
credits restored so that they would be sooner released
from prison to parole —even though parole would not
terminate the the State’s custody and would still include
significant constraints on their liberty.  See id. at 476,
500; see also Gov’t Br. 27-32.
Petitioner’s claim is the same  in all material respects.  He alleges that the Bureau of Prisons (BOP) has
unlawfully withheld time credits that, under  the First
Step Act , should  be applied toward his transfer to prerelease custody, and he seeks as a remedy the restoration of the credits and thus his earlier transfer out of
prison.  See Gov’t Br. 25.  As petitioner notes (Br. 25),
Preiser  “all but answers the question presented.”   Because petitioner is challenging the duration of his con-

4

finement  in prison and seeking to accelerate his transfer out of  prison, his claim sounds in habeas.   As petitioner notes, moreover (Br. 19), that understanding
draws textual support from the federal habeas statutes.
See 28 U.S.C. 2255(e) ( providing that a habeas claim is
available to a federal prisoner when a Section 2255 motion would be “ inadequate or ineffective to test the legality of his detention ”).
b. Amicus’s objections (Br. 37 -39) to that reasoning
are misplaced.  He faults us for “question begging” because “[a] halfway house falls in ‘a twilight zone between prison and freedom .’ ”  Br. 37 (quoting Ramsey v.
Brennan , 878 F.2d 995, 996 (7th Cir. 1989) (Posner, J.)).
But that is precisely the point .  A halfway house falls in
a “twilight zone between prison and freedom,” Ramsey,
878 F.2d at 996 (emphasis added), because  as a general
matter, such a facility  is not prison, as the governing
statutes make clear.  Gov’t Br. 29; see, e.g., 18 U.S.C.
3624(g)(5) ( authorizing revocation of prerelease custody
and return of the person to “prison”).  It is instead a setting that is more akin to parole or bail, forms of conditional release from prison that a habeas action has traditionally been used to obtain.   Our approach  rests on a
straightforward syllogism, not circular logic.
Amicus’s observation  (Br. 37) that  transfer to a halfway house  would leave petitioner  “in BOP custody at a
location ultimately controlled by BOP ” does not defeat
that syllogism .  Emphasizing  some discrete similarities
between halfway houses and prisons  only reinforces the
fact that the former are  “very different ” from the latter.
Woodall v. Federal Bureau of Prisons , 432 F.3d 235,
243 (3d Cir. 2005) .  We have already explained (Br. 27-
29) why BOP’s continued legal custody over individuals
in prerelease custody does not  make a difference with
respect to the availability of habeas.

5

Nor does BOP’s “ultimate control ” over persons  in
prerelease custody  render habeas unavailable  to seek
that form of transfer out of  prison.  The nature and extent of BOP’s control in the prerelease -custody setting
are significantly different from its control over inmates
in prison.  Cf. Admin. Off. of the U.S. Cts., Residential
Reentry Centers: Reference Guide  2 (Mar. 2020) (noting
that halfway houses “are operated by vendors under
contract” with BOP), https://www.uscourts.gov/file/28164/
download.  The government also maintains ultimate control over those who are on bail, parole, and supervised
release—which is why those forms of release are conditional rather than absolute .  See, e.g., Anderson  v. Corall, 263 U.S. 193, 196 (1923) (“ While on parole the convict is bound to remain in the legal custody and under
the control of the warden until the expiration of the
term.”).  Yet amicus accepts (Br. 14-15) that habeas is
available to seek release from prison or jail to th ose statuses.
In disputing our approach,  moreover, amicus conspicuously omits (see Br. 37 -39) any discussion of  the
other main form of prerelease custody , home confinement.  See 18 U.S.C. 3624 (g)(2).  It would blink reality
to equate residency in one’s own home—even subject to
the serious restrictions that home confinement entails,
see 18 U.S.C. 3624(g)(2)(A)—to prison.  And amicus does
not advance the counterintuitive proposition that habeas is available to seek transfer only to that form of
prerelease custody and not to a halfway house.
2. This case does not require a “level of custody” analysis
a. Amicus’s other main contention  (Br. 37-38) about
our prison-focused approach  is that some BOP prison
facilities —particularly federal prison camps —are so

6

low-security as to be similar to halfway houses  in certain respects.  But that hardly renders our “rule  *  * *
hopeless ly indeterminate,” contra Amicus Br. 38.   However permissive low-security prisons may be, they remain categorically  distinct from halfway houses and
home confinement.
For example, courts of appeals have held “[w]ithout
exception,” United States  v. Batts, 758 F.3d 915, 917
(8th Cir. 2014) (per curiam),  that prison camps are not
encompassed by Sentencing Guidelines §  2P1.1(b)(3),
which provides an offense -level reduction for a defendant convicted of  escape if he escaped from “a community
corrections center, community treatment center, ‘halfway house,’ or similar facility.”   Ibid.; s ee, e.g., Batts,
758 F.3d at 917; United States  v. Tapia, 981 F.2d 1194,
1197-1198 (11th Cir.)  (per curiam) , cert. denied, 508
U.S. 979 (1993) ; United States  v. Shaw, 979 F.2d 41, 44 -
45 (5th Cir.  1992); United States  v. Brownlee , 970 F.2d
764, 765 (10th Cir.  1992) (per curiam) ; United States v.
McGann, 960 F.2d 846, 847 (9th Cir.)  (per curiam) , cert.
denied, 506 U.S. 897 (1992).  Those courts have concluded
that p rison camps are “generically different  from the
facilities listed” in the guideline  and thus are not “ ‘similar facilit[ies] .’ ”  McGann, 960 F.2d at 847  (citation
omitted) .  A mong other reasons, halfway houses and
comparable facilities  are “integrated into the community,” whereas  “[a] prison camp, even though there may
be no perimeter barriers and residents may have some
freedom to come and go, is an environment separated
from the community .”  Brownlee , 970 F.2d at 765 ; see
Shaw, 979 F.2d at 45 (noting that “ the federal prison
camp’s purpose is to incarcerate the inmate while the
community center ’s purpose is to bring the inmate back
into society ”); 18 U.S.C. 3624(c)(1) (prerelease custody
is intended to “ afford th[e] prisoner a reasonable oppor-

7

tunity to adjust to and prepare for the reentry of that
prisoner into the community”).  There are also other “major difference[s] between the community center type facilities and a prison camp .”  Shaw, 979 F.2d at 43 ; see,
e.g., ibid. (contrasting halfway houses with prison camps
by noting that prisoners at one camp were “ counted at
least five times a day, six on weekends ,” were “ never
allowed unauthorized visitors ,” and had “strictly enforced” visiting hours ).
Thus, a prisoner’s claim demanding  transfer within a
prison system to a low -security facility is categorically
distinct from a claim , like petitioner’s,  demanding transfer to prerelease custody.  Only the latter type of claim
seeks “immediate or speedier release ” out of prison and
“into the community ,” which is the essence of a habeas
claim challenging unlawfully prolonged imprisonment .
Dotson, 544 U.S. at 82  (emphasis added).
b. The superficial similarities between halfway houses
and prison camps may not matte r at all under the view
of petitioner, who  proposes  (e.g., Br. 3-5, 12-20) that habeas encompasses claims challenging a prisoner’s  “level
of custody .”  That rule may mean that even claims seeking transfer to a lower security level within a prison or
prison system may be brought in habeas.   See, e.g., Graham v. Broglin, 922 F.2d 379, 381 (7th Cir. 1991) (Posner, J.) (contending that if a prisoner seeks “ the run of
the prison in contrast to the approximation to solitary
confinement that is disciplinary segregation ,” then “habeas corpus is his remedy”).  Under petitioner’s approach,
amicus’s e ffort to equate prerelease custody to imprisonment would not mean that petitioner’s claim does not
lie in habeas ; it may suggest only that claims seeking
transfer to less restrictive conditions of imprisonment
are also cognizable in habeas.

8

For several reasons, this  Court should not allow all
level-of-custody challenges to be brought in habeas .  It
is not necessary to do so  to resolve this case , since petitioner prevails under our narrower rule, which turns on
whether the claim seeks a transfer out of  prison.   Petitioner acknowledges as much .  See Br. 5 (describing his
claim as “seeking accelerated transfer from prison to
distinct and materially less restrictive custody served
outside of prison walls”);  Br. 18 (“a federal habeas court
may order the custodian to release the petitioner from
prison and transfer him to a lower level of custody”); Br.
24 (“habeas can be used to ‘free a petitioner from prison
custody’  ”) (brackets and citation omitted).
Contrary to petitioner’s suggestion (Br. 19 -29), t his
Court has not  already adopted a framework allowing
broad level-of-custody challenges in habeas .  Petitioner
cites precedents recognizing the availability of habeas
to secure bail or parole , but such claims  seek discharge
from prison or jail  (as does petitioner’s claim) , and thus
belong in habeas under our narrower rule .  See Br. 19-
26 (citing, e.g., Ex parte Bollman , 4 Cranch 75 (1807) ;
Ex parte Hull , 312 U.S. 546 (1941) ; and Preiser , supra);
see also Jones v. Hendrix, 599 U.S. at 475 (contemplating a habeas claim that a prisoner “has unlawfully been
denied parole or good-time credits”).  As amicus explains
(Br. 23), In re Bonner , 151 U.S. 242 (1894),  held that
habeas was available to challenge imprisonment that
was not authorized by statute , which is not a level -ofcustody claim.
Nor do th is Court’s modern cases hold that habeas
encompasses all level -of-custody claims , contra Pet. Br.
25-29.  No such claim was raised in Skinner v. Switzer,
562 U.S. 521 (2011), wh ich held that 42 U.S.C. 1983 rather than habeas was the proper vehicle for a state prisoner’s claim seeking DNA testing of crime -scene evi-

9

dence.  See 562 U.S. at 534.  The Court did indicate that
habeas is not “the sole remedy, or even an available one,
where the relief sought would ‘neither terminate custody, accelerate the future date of release from custody,
nor reduce the level of custody .’ ”  Ibid. (emphasis added;
brackets and citation omitted) .  But the Court was quoting Justice Scalia’s concurring opinion in Dotson, which
suggested only that a “  ‘quantum change in the level of
custody ,’ such as release from incarceration to parole ,”
is “permissible habeas relief .”  544 U.S. at 86  (quoting
Graham, 922 F.2d at 381)  (emphases added) ; see Amicus Br. 26 .  Similarly far afield are cases  involving the
use of habeas to challenge a sentence  of death , see Hill
v. McDonough , 547 U.S. 573 , 583 (2006), or to block a
detainee’s transfer out of the country, see Trump v.
J.G.G., 604 U.S. 670 , 672 (2025) (per curiam); id. at 674
(Kavanaugh, J., concurring).
Allowing all level-of-custody claims to proceed in habeas would be in tension with this Court’s precedents.
As amicus notes, the Court has allowed state prisoners
to proceed under Section 1983  when challenging their
placements in prison environments  that are more restrictive .  Br. 35 (citing Haines v. Kerner, 404 U.S. 519
(1972) (per curiam) , and Meachum v. Fano, 427 U.S. 215
(1976)).  Such claims , unlike petitioner’s,  are difficult  to
distinguish from other challenges to prisoners’  “conditions of confinement,” which likely are not cognizable in
habeas.  See Amicus Br. 16 -20; see also Muhammad  v.
Close, 540 U.S. 749, 751 n.1 (2004) (per curiam) .  Thus,
unlike our rule, a broad level -of-custody approach
would risk making the scope of habeas as “hopelessly
indeterminate” as amicus fears (Br. 38).  For this case,
it suffices to apply th e Court’s precedents holding that
a claim challeng ing unlawfully prolonged imprisonment

10

and seek ing accelerated transfer out of  prison into the
community  sounds in habeas.
B. Petitioner Would Prevail Even Under Amicus’s Approach
1. Prerelease custody in a halfway house or home confinement is not “physical detention ”
Amicus instead proposes the following standard:  a
“prisoner’s claim sounds in habeas” if it “implies [1] that
his physical detention must be shortened or terminated,
[2] that he is entitled to earlier release on bail or parole,
or [3] that the sentencing court ordered him to serve his
sentence in a place it did not have jurisdiction to send
him.”  Amicus Br. 20; see id. at 21-23.  Yet that framework would yield the same result as ours in this case .
Petitioner’s claim is that his physical detention in prison
must be shortened based on his First Step Act time
credits and that he is therefore entitled to accelerated
transfer  out of prison to prerelease custody.
Amicus’s disagreement with that logic rests on the
premise that someone in prerelease custody remains in
physical detention.  But p rerelease custody in a halfway
house or home confinement is not “physical detention”
under any ordinary  understanding  of that term.   Prerelease custody does not depend on physical restraints or
barriers, but rather on the releasee’s compliance with
restrictions on his liberty: the rules and regulations of
the halfway house, for example, or  the restrictions for
home confinement imposed by the First Step Act and
BOP.  See 18 U.S.C. 3624(g)(2) .  That is why amicus describes (Br. 23 , 37 ) BOP as retaining “ultimate[]” control over prisoners in prerelease custody.   Cf. Black’s
Law Dictionary  1384 (12th ed. 2024) (defining “physical
custody” as “[c] ustody of a person (such as an arrestee)

11

whose freedom is directly controlled and limited ”) (emphasis added) .
Amicus’s view also cannot be reconciled with precedent.  In light of the practical similarities  for present
purposes  between prerelease custody, parole , and bail,
see pp. 12-16, infra, amicus is compelled to place  (Br.
20) claims seeking parole or bail in a separate , second
category o f cognizable habeas claims —necessarily implying that he views parole and bail as entailing continued “physical detention” as well.   But this Court has not
taken that view.  In 1963, it recognized the basic distinction between parole —despite its attendant “significant
restraints on [parolees’]  liberty”—and “actual, physical
custody,” “physical confinement,” and “physical imprisonment.”  Jones v. Cunningham , 371 U.S. at 238, 240,
242; see id. at 243 (the “ writ always could and still can
reach behind prison walls and iron bars ”).  Ten years
later, the Court in Preiser did the same , holding that a
claim seeking release from prison to parole must be
brought in habeas.  The Court’s core reason for that
holding was that such a claim seeks to terminate  unlawful “physical restraint,” “physical confinement,” and
“physical custody.”   Preiser, 411 U.S. at 486 -487.
Amicus accordingly errs (Br. 25) in dismissing Preiser
as pertaining only to “release on parole .”  Preiser did
not turn on the particular ities of parole —it did not even
discuss them .  It instead rested on the more general
principle, which this Court had recognized before
Preiser , that a claim sounds in habeas if it alleges “illegal physical confinement” and demands “release from
physical custody” as a remedy.  411 U.S. at 487; see id.
at 489-490, 494, 500; see also Jones v. Cunningham , 371
U.S. at 238.  That principle also governs this case.
Indeed, i t is telling that amicus derives his own
“physical detention” category from Preiser itself.  See

12

Amicus Br. 21 (“Claims that would result in ‘immediate
release from physical custody’ or ‘discharge from any
confinement contrary to the Constitution or fundamental law’ are paradigmatic habeas claims.”) (quoting
Preiser, 411 U.S. at 485 -487).  Over the decades, Preiser
and its progeny have guided the Court’s analysis of the
scope of habeas in a range of cases —including several
that did not involv e parole at all.  See, e.g., Fernandez
v. United States , 608 U.S. 411, 420 -423 (2026); Nance v.
Ward, 597 U.S. 159, 167 -168 (2022); see also Dotson, 544
U.S. at 78 -82.  This Court’s decisions “are ‘governed by
general principles, rather than ad hoc improvisations.’  ”
Trinity Lutheran Church of Columbia, Inc.  v. Comer,
582 U.S. 449, 470 (2017) (Gorsuch, J., concurring in part)
(quoting Elk Grove Unified Sch. Dist.  v. Newdow, 542
U.S. 1, 25 (2004) (Rehnquist, C.J., concurring in the
judgment)).
In short, c laims seeking parole or bail  do not, as amicus would have it (Br. 20),  compose a freestanding category of cognizable habeas claims .  They are instead examples of claims that sound in habeas because they seek
release from “physical detention .”  Because petitioner’s
claim falls comfortably within that category , he would
prevail under amicus’s  own framework.
2. Prerelease custody is materially similar to parole
and supervised release
Even if amicus were correct that prerelease custody
in a halfway house or home confinement entails continued physical detention, there would be no principled basis for distinguishing petitioner’s claim from claims that
seek release to parole or supervised release  or bail.
There are various significant differences among all of
those forms of conditional release .  See, e.g. , United
States v. Haymond, 588 U.S. 634, 652 (2019) (plurality

13

opinion) (“ ‘unlike parole, ’ supervised release wasn ’t introduced to replace a portion of the defendant ’s prison
term, only to encourage rehabilitation after the completion of his prison term ”) (brackets and citation omitted) .
For instance, a  defendant on pretrial bail  differs from
someone on parole or supervised release because he has
not yet been convicted of a crim e.  Y et amicus accepts
that habeas is available for someone seeking those forms
of release , no twithstanding their differences .  The distinctive characteristics of prerelease custody do not
support a different result here.
By statute,  amicus observes  (Br. 29), a person in prerelease custody is still “serving a term of imprison ment”
and is referred to as a “prisoner,” 18 U.S.C. 3624(c)(1), unlike someone on supervised release.  But several statutory provisions illustrate that Congress distinguished
between being in prison and being in prerel ease custody—including  by authorizing  BOP to “revoke the
prisoner’s prerelease custody and require the prisoner
to serve the remainder of the term of imprisonment
* * *  in prison .”  18 U.S.C. 3624(g)(5); s ee Gov’t Br. 29-
30.  Moreover, what matters is not the terminological
point, but the substantive difference.  Whether a claim
sounds in habeas depends not on labels but on  the nature of “the allegations made” and “the relief sought.”
Olivier v. City of Brandon , 607 U.S. 552, 566 (2026).   In
this regard, a micus’s citation  (Br. 29)  of United States
v. Johnson, 529 U.S. 53 (2000), undermines his own argument.   Johnson held that a term of supervised release
begins only once a prisoner is actually  released from
prison, not when his term of imprisonment should have
ended.  See id. at 56-60.  Our approach likewise focuses
on release from actual imprisonment , consistent with
this Court’s habeas precedents.

14

Amicus further attempts (Br. 30) to distinguish prerelease custody and supervised release based on “the
severity of restrictions on liberty”  that each status imposes.  As we have explained (Gov’t Br. 30 -31), a categorical distinction between prerelease custody and supervised release is un tenable.  I ndividuals on supervised release can be subject to restrictions on their liberty that are equal to or even greater than those that
apply to prerelease custody.  Compare Sentencing Guidelines § 5D1.3(b)(2) (conditions of supervised release),
with, e.g., 18 U.S.C. 3624 (g)(2)(A) (conditions of prerelease custody in home confinement).   The relative restrictiveness  will depend on various individualized determinations .  For example, the  First Step Act requires
BOP, “to the extent practicable, [to] provide that increasingly less restrictive conditions shall be imposed
on prisoners” in prerelease custody “who demonstrate
continued compliance with the conditions of such prerelease custody, so as to most effectively prepare such
prisoners for reentry.”  18 U.S.C. 3624(g)(4).   And a s
amicus acknowledges (Br. 31-32), many terms of supervised release are served in the very same environments
where prisoners spend prerelease custody.  See Sentencing Guidelines § 5D1.3(b)(3)(K)  (“Residence in a community treatment center, halfway house or similar facility may be imposed as a condition of supervised release.”).
Amicus also emphasizes (Br. 30-31) that supervised
release is overseen by the Judicial Branch (through sentencing courts and probation officers), whereas prerelease custody is overseen by the Executive Branch
(through BOP).   But t hat too is a distinction without a
difference , since parole has also been overseen by the
Executive Branch.  See Mistretta  v. United States , 488
U.S. 361, 364-365 (1989); Knight v. United States , 73

15

F.3d 117, 120 (7th Cir. 1995) ( “The Parole Commission
supervises the paroled convict  and may at any time,
upon notice and hearing, change the conditions of the
parole, revoke it or even terminate it entirely. ”) (citation omitted) , cert. denied, 519 U.S. 827 (1996).
This Court’s decision in Reno v. Koray, 515 U.S. 50
(1995), does not support amicus’s effort (Br. 32 -34) to
distinguish prerelease custody from supervised release
for habeas purposes.  Koray held that a defendant who
is ordered “released” on bail subject to the condition
that he reside in a halfway house is not in “official detention” for purposes of a sentencing -credit statute, 18
U.S.C. 3585(b), even though a defendant who is “detained” in the custody of BOP could be placed in the
same environment  and earn such credit.  See 515 U.S. at
62, 65.  That result was not as anomalous as it appeared,
the Court explained, because the difference between released and detained defendants had “legal and practical
significance ”:  for instance, a released defendant “ is not
in BOP ’s custody ” and  “cannot be summarily reassigned to a different place of confinement unless a judicial officer revokes his release .”  Id. at 63.
Koray did not involve  or address  prerelease custody
or the scope of habeas , so its reasoning sheds little light
on the question presented in this case .  The “legal and
practical significance” of BOP custody for the “official
detention” issue of statutory  interpretation in Koray,
515 U.S. at 63,  does not suggest that it has the same
significance with respect to the availability of habeas.
The precedents discussed above show that it does not.
As we have explained, BOP’s continued legal custody
over prisoners in prerelease custody cannot control the
habeas analysis.  See Gov’t Br. 27-29.  While amicus’s distinctions between prerelease custody and other forms of

16

conditional release from prison may matter for other legal purposes , they are immaterial here.
C. Amicus Identifies No Other Plausible Avenues For First
Step Act Time -Credit Claims
Furthermore, as we previously explained (Br. 32 -35),
for claims like petitioner’s, there is no potential avenue
that is more suitable than habeas.  Amicus recognizes
(Br. 41)  that the court of appeals  “was mistaken” when
asserting “that federal prisoners like [p]etitioner might
be able to proceed under Bivens .”  See J.A. 35.  Petitioner is  not suing for damages or raising a constitutional claim , and this Court is very unlikely to extend
Bivens to a new type of claim —particularly one arising
in the prison setting.  See , e.g., Goldey v. Fields, 606
U.S. 942, 944-945 (2025) (per curiam); see  generally U.S.
Amicus Br. at 11-21, Nielsen v. Watanabe, cert. granted,
No. 25-417 (oral argument scheduled for Nov. 9, 2026 ).
The other avenues for relief discussed by amicus are
only marginally  more plausible than a Bivens suit.  His
leading candidate is a suit “in equity for an injunction.”
Br. 40 (citing Armstrong v. Exceptional Child Ctr., Inc. ,
575 U.S. 320, 327 (2015)).   But First Step Act claims like
petitioner’s are not constitutional claims  (unlike most
conditions -of-confinement claims) , see Gov’t Br. 34; cf.
Armstrong , 575 U.S. at 327, so amicus must have in
mind an ultra vires  claim alleging governmental action
“in excess of  * * *  statutory authority ,” Dalton v. Specter, 511 U.S. 462, 472 (1994).   Such a claim requires a
showing that “an agency has taken action entirely ‘in excess of its delegated powers and contrary to a  specific
prohibition ’ in a statute ,” and is thus “ ‘essentially a
Hail Mary pass’  ” that “ ‘rarely succeeds.’  ”  Nuclear Regulatory Comm’n v. Texas, 605 U.S. 665, 681-682 (2025)
(citations omitted).

17

It is difficult to imagine a First Step Act claim that
could clear that exceptionally high bar.  Claims like petitioner’s allege that BOP has failed to discharge affirmative duties under the Act to grant time credits and
transfer eligible prisoners to prerelease custody, not
that the agency has violated any specific statutory prohibition.   Cf. Nuclear Regulatory Comm’n , 605 U.S. at
681.  Permitting such claims would be particularly inappropriate because, as amicus acknowledges (Br. 42), it
would allow prisoners to circumvent “the host of substantive and procedural limitations that Congress has
imposed on habeas petitioners.”  See Pet. Br. 32-33; Gov’t
Br. 34-35.
Amicus briefly suggests (Br. 41) that prisoners
“may” also be able to bring First Step Act claims via the
Administrative Procedure Act  (APA), 5 U.S.C. 701 et
seq.   Petitioner  himself considers (Br. 31) it “unclear”
whether the APA would work.  But Congress has clearly
precluded APA review .  I t provided in 18 U.S.C. 3625
that the APA “ do[es] not apply to the making of any determination, decision, or order under th is subchapter ,”
ibid., which includes the provisions of the First Step Act
governing prisoners’ transfer s to prerelease custody, 18
U.S.C. 3 621 and 3624.   See Sills v. FCI Talladega Warden, No. 22-12656, 2023 WL 1775725 , at *4 n.3 (11th Cir.
Feb. 6, 2023) (per curiam)  (“§ 3625 expressly exempts
the BOP ’s prisoner -placement and prerelease -custody
decisions, including home confinement, from judicial review under the  [APA]”).  And a mandamus action under
28 U.S.C. 1361 (see Amicus Br. 41) would likely fail for
the same reasons that an ultra vires  claim would , given
that “only exceptional circumstances amounting to a judicial usurpation of power or a clear abuse of discretion
will justify” mandamus .  Cheney v. United States Dist.
Ct., 542 U.S. 367, 380 (2004)  (citations and internal quo-

18

tation marks omitted).   The absence of any other suitable avenue for bringing a claim like petitioner’s confirms that habeas, contrary to the decision below, would
be the right one.
D. The Fifth Circuit’s Judgment Should Be Vacated
1. In the end,  however,  the foregoing  is beside the
point if  the First Step Act , in 18 U.S.C. 3621(b),  has
foreclosed judicial review of BOP’s decisions regarding
transfers to prerelease custody , as we contend (Br. 36 -
40) and the Eighth Circuit recently  held.  See 18 U.S.C.
3621(b) ( “Notwithstanding any other provision of law, a
designation of a place of imprisonment under this subsection is not reviewable by any court. ”); Osorio-Calderon v. Warden, 179 F.4th 1158, 1163-1165 (8th Cir. 2026).
Amicus seems to agree , stating that “Congress appears
to have barred” claims like petitioner’s in Section 3621(b).
Amicus Br. 40; see id. at 41.
Although certain congressional amici disagree with
that view, their arguments lack merit.  They observe
that Section 3621(b) refers to BOP’s designation of the
place of imprisonment “under this subsection,” and they
suggest that a prisoner’s placement in prerelease custody under the First Step Act is controlled  exclusively
by other statutory provisions  “governing whether someone has become eligible for prerelease custody ,” such as
Section 3624.   Sens. Durbin and Booker Am icus Br. 12
n.4; see Rep. Raskin Amicus Br. 13-14.  But, as we have
explained and  “[p]etitioner’s own habeas petition ”
acknowledges  (Gov’t Br. 37), Section 3624 does not displace Section 3621(b) .  See, e.g., 18 U.S.C. 3624 (c)(6)(A)
(requiring BOP to “ensure that placement in a community correctional facility” is “ conducted in a manner consistent with section 3621(b) ”).

19

A contrary reading “would result in troubling anomalies” that would not “accord[ ] with the statutory
scheme.”  Boggs v. Boggs, 520 U.S. 833, 850 -851 (1997).
For example, BOP could be forced to place prisoners in
prerelease custody  under the First Step Act without regard for the placement considerations listed in Section
3621(b), such as “ the prisoner’s security designation,
the prisoner’s programmatic needs, the prisoner’s mental and medical health needs ,” “other security concerns
of the  Bureau of Prisons,”  “minimum standards of
health and habitability established by the Bureau ,” and
other important factors .  18 U.S.C. 3621(b); cf. Epic Sys.
Corp. v. Lewis, 584 U.S. 497, 510 (2018) (“ When confronted with two Acts of Congress allegedly touching on
the same topic, this Court is not at liberty to pick and
choose among congressional enactments and must instead strive to give effect to both .”) (citation and internal quotation marks omitted).   If amici were correct, a
court could order BOP to transfer a prisoner to prerelease custody even if there were no facilities  with space
for him , or if the only available facilities  were plainly
inappropriate for the prisoner —for instance, facilities
located near schools, in the case of a prisoner with a history of sex offenses against children.   Section 3621(b)
thus plays an essential role in BOP’s ability to responsibly implement the First Step Act’s risk -and-needs-assessment system, of which the time -credit incentive
program is a central part.
Some amici also emphasize the First Step Act’s “mandatory language” requiring BOP to place eligible prisoners in prerelease custody.  Sen s. Durbin and Booker
Amicus Br. 12 n.4; see  18 U.S.C. 36 32(d)(4) (C) (“The Director of the Bureau of Prisons shall transfer eligible
prisoners, as determined under section 3624(g), into
prerelease custody or supervised release. ”) (emphasis

20

added).  But Congress’s use of mandatory language is
not inconsistent with its preclusion of judicial review as
a means to enforce the mandate on the agency.  See, e.g.,
Mullin v. Doe, 609 U.S. 324 (2026).   That is particularly
so where, as here, Congress has provided other mechanisms for oversight of the agency’s implementation of
the statute.  For example, the First Step Act directs the
Attorney General to “develop and implement training
programs for Bureau of Prisons officers and employees
responsible for administering the [risk-and-needs-assessment ] System,” 18 U.S.C. 3632(f  ), and to “ ensure
that the Bureau of Prisons is using the System in an appropriate and consistent manner ” by “monitor[ing] and
assess[ing] the use of the System, which shall include
conducting annual audits of the Bureau of Prisons regarding the use of the System ,” 18 U.S.C. 3632(g).   The
Act likewise directs the Comptroller General to conduct
an audit every two years, including of “[w] hether the
Bureau of Prisons transfers prisoners to prerelease
custody or supervised release as soon as they are eligible for such a transfer .”  § 103 (7), 132 Stat. 5214.   Congress understandably viewed those means of oversight
as more appropriate than judicial enforcement  in this
context.
2. If our reading of Section 3621(b) is correct, the
question presented in this case “will be essentially academic.”  Gov’t Br. 41.  E ven though a prisoner like petitioner could theoretically bring a First Step Act time -
credit claim via habeas , that claim would be barred by
Section 3621(b) , which applies “[n]otwithstanding any
other provision of law .”  18 U.S.C. 3621(b) .  Resolution
of the question presented is also likely to be academic
for petitioner  himself.  Even under the BOP calculation
of time credits  that he challenges, h e is currently scheduled to be eligible for transfer to a halfway house in Jan-

21

uary 2027, see Gov’t Br. 14, 41, which would render moot
his habeas claim for an earlier transfer .
For those reasons, this Court may wish to dismiss
the writ of certiorari as improvidently granted .  The
scope of habeas corpus is a recurring issue , see, e.g.,
J.G.G., 604 U.S. at 672; Olivier, 607 U.S. at 562-564, that
is important at both the federal and state levels.  It is
therefore especially appropriate for the Court to reserve decisions in this area for cases in which they will
have practical consequences.  But if the Court does not
dismiss , the appropriate disposition is vacatur and remand for further proceedings.

should be vacated .
